title: Receiving Feedback About Bias and Making a Useful Repair
before: Explore how DSD staff hear a specific concern about bias, examine their own part, and make a useful, proportionate repair.

turns.text: This course is Receiving Feedback About Bias and Making a Useful Repair. It’s about the moment someone tells you that a phrase, a decision, or an interaction may have carried bias, and you notice your own reaction. The course starts by separating two questions that can feel like one: a concern about a specific action, and a judgment about your whole character.

And it’s honest about discomfort. Discomfort tells you the message is hard to receive. It doesn’t tell you whether the factual concern is true or false. A respectful response can include accountability and, where it’s warranted, a precise factual disagreement. The work is to return attention to the wording, decision, or interaction itself.

The opening case is about a service draft. A community participant says it describes families as irresponsible when a step is incomplete. Staff want to explain that the intention was to encourage action. You’ll practice choosing a response. As you do, consider what the sentence actually establishes, and whether an intention to help settles what the wording implies.

The course suggests an opening that keeps the concern available. Name the specific concern before explaining yourself. Saying “I hear that the sentence assigns a motive we have not established” does more than a defense of good intentions. It also separates clarification from cross-examination. One helps identify what needs correction. The other tries to defeat the person who raised it.

I like the example about precision. You can disagree with one detail and still own another part of the action. “I did not draft the sentence, but I approved its use” keeps the fact and the responsibility together. That’s very different from using a factual point to step away from the whole concern.

The supervision practice situation tests this. An employee says comparable work received different performance feedback, and the supervisor finds the concern uncomfortable. You’ll consider the most useful next response. The course notes that a concern like this calls for specific evidence and relevant criteria, and that the appropriate review responsibilities still apply.

Then apology and repair. An apology names the action and the part you own. A repair addresses the effect on a record, a decision, or an opportunity, and it should be proportionate and feasible. Forgiveness and reassurance aren’t conditions for making a needed correction. The person may say more, ask for another route, or decline discussion.

Privacy shapes the repair, too. In the third practice situation, a shared summary credits a community contributor’s idea to someone else, and the contributor raises the concern privately. You’ll decide what repair fits the evidence. The course notes that a private account shouldn’t be repeated to make an apology seem more convincing.

Follow-through is where repair becomes real. Check whether the promised correction happened and whether the practice changed, because a convincing apology isn’t the same evidence. It also helps to offer an update without seeking praise or repeatedly asking the person to confirm your growth. That can quietly put the burden back on them.

The course also looks beyond one conversation. If concerns are routinely met with dismissal, extra proof demands, or judgments about reputation, people may stop raising useful information. Then the absence of complaints can’t establish fairness. Near the end, you’ll privately rewrite a defensive response: “That is not what I meant, and I have always supported equity.”

As you go, think about a time you received feedback that was hard to hear. What was the specific action? What helped you return to it, or what got in the way? Bring that example with you privately. The course offers a way to receive the next concern with more steadiness and a clearer sense of what to do.

guidance.title: Discomfort as a signal
guidance.text: Feeling defensive when someone raises a concern is common, and it does not mean you did something wrong. It also does not mean you did not. Treat the feeling as a signal to slow down. Ask yourself what specific action the person named, and what you would need to look at to understand it. That keeps your attention on the concern rather than on your reputation.

guidance.title: What you would say next
guidance.text: Read your rewritten response again. Does it name the action before it explains your intention? If you included a factual disagreement, is it precise, and does it still leave your responsibility visible? Consider whether anything in your response asks the other person for reassurance. What would a feasible next step look like, and how would you follow through on it?
